source.title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
source.authors: Sukrut Rao; S. Mahajan; Moritz Böhle; B. Schiele

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures human-rated semantic consistency of top-activating examples for CLIP feature neurons and compares them with sparse-autoencoder features. This is a different measurement from the cited neuron-interpretability work, but bears on whether individual vision features have coherent meanings.
record.gate_note: The user study is the relevant result: it rates semantic consistency and name accuracy for sampled features using top-activating images. Other concept-bottleneck classification and intervention results do not measure neuron polysemanticity. Claims about prior work are citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: This is a concept-bottleneck method paper. It takes as given that individual neurons are often polysemantic and uses sparse autoencoders, a tool built on the superposition idea, to get more interpretable concepts. Its only neuron-level result is a user study in which 9 sampled CLIP ResNet-50 output-embedding dimensions, named with CLIP-Dissect, serve as a baseline against 15 SAE nodes. The CLIP ratings appear only in Fig. 4, with no numbers. A low 'semantic consistency' rating does not show that a neuron responds to several unrelated inputs. The paper reports its own method's performance against that baseline rather than testing whether polysemantic neurons exist or why they arise.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that SAEs discover concepts in CLIP that are semantically consistent and can be named automatically, and that these concepts give performant, interpretable, task-agnostic CBMs. The comparison with raw CLIP features is offered as support for the SAE approach, not as a finding about polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: This is a sparse-autoencoder concept-discovery and human-rating study, not a reproduction of the original neuron-level method. It compares SAE nodes with CLIP feature neurons using sampled top-activating images and human judgments.
record.method_sensitivity: Semantic consistency decreases as alignment between a feature's dictionary vector and its assigned text embedding decreases; the comparison also varies between SAE nodes and CLIP feature neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 22-respondent user study, sampled SAE nodes trained on CLIP ResNet-50 output features were rated more semantically consistent and better named than sampled raw CLIP output dimensions named by CLIP-Dissect. Ratings fell with lower name alignment for both (Fig. 4, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-autoencoder features of a vision encoder are more semantically coherent than the encoder's raw feature dimensions.

record.problems: The neuron comparison uses only 9 sampled CLIP features and the SAE assessment only 15 sampled nodes, judged by a user study with 22 responses. Ratings are shown in a figure without reported numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The evaluation uses top-activating images and semantic-consistency judgments, which do not directly establish whether a neuron's mixed inputs are unrelated.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted. Classification accuracy, concept interventions, qualitative clusters, and the SUNAttributes score do not directly measure individual-neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Whether individual vision-model neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. The study only rates the consistency of top images for 9 CLIP output dimensions, as a baseline, with no numbers reported.
Language-model MLP neurons are not studied.
Superposition as the cause is cited (Elhage et al., Bricken et al.) and assumed, not tested.
Not studied. The ViT and ResNet backbones are compared only on classification accuracy.
Not studied as a property of neurons. The alignment bins sort units by how well they were named, not by measurement choices about the activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's label (V1 limits_scope on R1–R3) is dropped. These rows are a figure-only method baseline on output-embedding dimensions of a CLIP model, not hidden neurons of an image classifier, and the measure cannot show unrelated mixtures. The paper's mentions of polysemanticity and superposition are citations of prior work.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests sampled CLIP ResNet-50 feature neurons, not InceptionV1 or the cited neuron 4e:55; it does not establish that their activating inputs are unrelated in the specific sense of the claim.
Language models and transformer MLP neurons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons, or whether capacity pressure causes it.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The effect of activation function, architecture, or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons, and whether that share can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated mixtures.
The study uses top-activating images and varies feature-alignment groups, but does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods as a test of measurement dependence.

rows.subject: CLIP ResNet-50 image feature vector
rows.operation_detail: Human raters scored semantic consistency of top-activating images for sampled feature neurons.

conditions.value: top four activating images each from ImageNet, Places365, and CC3M

rows.measure: Five-point human rating of whether the top-activating images share a semantically consistent, human-interpretable concept.
rows.note: The text reports that consistency decreases as alignment decreases and that CLIP features are less interpretable than SAE features overall, but gives no numerical score for this bin. Semantic consistency ratings do not specifically determine whether mixtures are unrelated.
rows.check: Baseline in a method comparison, not a test of V1. The subject is the pooled 1024-d CLIP output embedding, not hidden neurons of an image classifier like InceptionV1. The value is figure-only, and a consistency rating cannot show unrelated mixtures.
